```{r}
#| label: setup
library(opencodecounts)
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(scales)
library(here)
library(patchwork)
library(paletteer)

OCC_GP_DATA_VERSION <- "0.2.0"
OCC_PACKAGE_VERSION <- as.character(packageVersion("opencodecounts"))

dir.create(here("output", "figures"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(here("output", "tables"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

df_snomed_usage <- get_gp_snomed(version = OCC_GP_DATA_VERSION)
```

```{r}
#| label: get-codelists

# Download the codelists in codelists.txt and save them as CSV files
ids <- read_lines(here("codelists", "codelists.txt"))
codelists <- map(set_names(ids, str_replace_all(dirname(ids), "/", "-")), \(id) {
  get_codelist(paste0("https://www.opencodelists.org/codelist/", id))
})
iwalk(codelists, \(x, name) write_csv(x, here("codelists", paste0(name, ".csv"))))

df_anx_proms_cod <- codelists[["user-Lola_O-proms-anx"]]
df_anx_proms_declined_cod <- codelists[["user-Lola_O-proms-anx-declined"]]
df_dep_proms_cod <- codelists[["user-Lola_O-proms-dep"]]
df_dep_proms_declined_cod <- codelists[["user-Lola_O-proms-dep-declined"]]
```

```{r}
#| label: load-functions
source(here("lib", "usage-functions.R"))
source(here("lib", "helper-functions.R"))
source(here("lib", "dictionaries.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tidy-occ-data
START_DATE <- min(df_snomed_usage$start_date)
END_DATE <- max(df_snomed_usage$end_date)

# Keep study codes, count inactive codes as their linked active code, and use
# the latest description for each code
df_anx_dep_snomed_usage <- df_snomed_usage |>
  filter(snomed_code %in% unlist(map(codelists, "code"))) |>
  combine_linked_codes(dict_linked_codes) |>
  mutate(
    semantic_tag = extract_semantic_tag(description),
    description_short = strip_semantic_tag(description)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    description_short = last(description_short, order_by = end_date),
    .by = snomed_code
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(end_date), snomed_code)
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-datasets
# One row per code and codelist
df_anx_dep_codelist_lookup <- codelists |>
  map(\(codelist) tibble(snomed_code = codelist$code)) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "codelist") |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(
    condition = if_else(str_detect(codelist, "anx"), "anx", "dep"),
    type = if_else(str_detect(codelist, "declined"), "declined", "activity")
  )

# One row per code, period and codelist. Codes in both conditions appear twice.
df_anx_dep_usage <- df_anx_dep_snomed_usage |>
  inner_join(
    df_anx_dep_codelist_lookup,
    by = "snomed_code",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    condition_label = factor(
      condition,
      levels = names(dict_condition_labels),
      labels = dict_condition_labels
    )
  )

# Total usage per code, with each code's share of its condition
df_anx_dep_overall <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  summarise(
    overall_usage = sum(usage),
    .by = c(condition, type, snomed_code, description_short, semantic_tag)
  ) |>
  mutate(share_usage = overall_usage / sum(overall_usage), .by = condition)

# Yearly usage per code for the results text
df_anx_dep_events <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  mutate(year = year(end_date)) |>
  summarise(
    usage = sum(usage),
    .by = c(condition, type, semantic_tag, snomed_code, year)
  )

x_breaks <- sort(unique(df_anx_dep_usage$end_date))

df_anx_events <- filter(df_anx_dep_events, condition == "anx")
df_dep_events <- filter(df_anx_dep_events, condition == "dep")
```


## Abstract

```{r}
#| label: abstract
txt_anx_overall <- usage_total(df_anx_events)
txt_dep_overall <- usage_total(df_dep_events)

txt_dep_last <- usage_total(df_dep_events, year == year(END_DATE))
txt_anx_last <- usage_total(df_anx_events, year == year(END_DATE))

txt_dep_anx_ratio_overall_rounded <- round(
  usage_total(df_dep_events, .format_as_str = FALSE) /
    usage_total(df_anx_events, .format_as_str = FALSE)
)
txt_dep_anx_ratio_last_rounded <- round(
  usage_total(df_dep_events, year == year(END_DATE), .format_as_str = FALSE) /
    usage_total(df_anx_events, year == year(END_DATE), .format_as_str = FALSE),
  1
)
```

**Background:**
Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are widely used to assess symptom severity, guide treatment, and inform service improvement for anxiety disorders and depression in mental health settings.
However, PROMs use is not systematic in primary care, where most individuals with these conditions first present.
**Aim:**
To describe PROMs recording and use from `r format(START_DATE, "%B %Y")` to `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` for anxiety disorders and depression in primary care electronic health records in England.
**Design and setting:**
Retrospective descriptive analysis of publicly available national SNOMED CT code usage data from most general practices in England through OpenCodeCounts.
**Method:**
We developed PROMs activity and declined-assessment codelists for anxiety disorders and depression, described code usage, and plotted annual trends.
**Results:**
Over the past 5 years, GAD-7 and PHQ-9 were the most frequently recorded PROMs for anxiety disorders and depression, respectively.
Recording shifted from PROMs procedure codes, which do not record assessment scores, towards PROMs codes that record these measure scores.
Over the entire study period, depression-related PROMs codes were recorded around `r txt_dep_anx_ratio_overall_rounded` times as often as anxiety disorder-related codes (`r txt_dep_overall` vs `r txt_anx_overall`), decreasing to `r txt_dep_anx_ratio_last_rounded` times in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (`r txt_dep_last` vs `r txt_anx_last`).
PHQ-9 score usage dropped by half after 2013, following the cessation of financial incentives to record them. This fall was recovered completely by `r year(END_DATE)`.
**Conclusion:**
Publicly available aggregate data can be used to describe PROMs recording over time, explore trends, and inform feasibility of research on anxiety disorders and depression in English general practice.

**Keywords:** patient-reported outcome measures, anxiety disorders, depression, primary care, SNOMED CT, electronic health records

## How this fits in

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the British Medical Association (BMA) recommend the use of patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) for assessing symptom severity in anxiety disorders and depression.
How often and in what form these measures are recorded in general practice is unclear.
We used OpenCodeCounts, an openly accessible online tool and R package that shows how often clinical codes are used in England.
Over the past 5 years, recording shifted towards codes that record the measure scores, specifically PHQ-9 and GAD-7.
Additionally, recording of PHQ-9 declined after financial incentives ended in 2013, before increasing again by the end of the study period in `r year(END_DATE)`.
These findings provide national context on PROMs recording in primary care.
They also show how publicly available data can inform future patient-level studies.

## Introduction

Anxiety disorders and depression are the most common mental health conditions in England.
The nationally representative Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey found that the prevalence of generalised anxiety disorder and depressive episodes among adults aged 16-64 increased between 1993 and 2023/24, reaching 8.5% and 4.4% respectively [@Morris2025].
Recorded anxiety disorder diagnoses and symptoms in primary care have similarly increased [@Archer2022; @Slee2021].
Primary care is the main point of contact for people with anxiety disorders and depression in England [@Morris2025].
Psychological (talking) therapies are recommended for these conditions, with most therapy in England provided by NHS Talking Therapies (NHS TT) for anxiety and depression, which treated over 674,000 adults in 2025-26 [@Clark2018a; @NHSEngland2026].
In both settings, structured assessment of symptom severity guides clinical decisions, including identifying appropriate treatment and monitoring progress [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020; @NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2022].

Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) are self-completed questionnaires that assess symptom severity and daily functioning in physical and mental health conditions.
They are used across primary, secondary, and community-based care [@Kendir2025].
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the British Medical Association (BMA) recommend validated measures to assess severity and guide treatment decisions [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020; @NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2022; @BritishMedicalAssociation2006].
For depression, the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 [PHQ-9, @Kroenke2001], the Beck Depression Inventory [BDI-II, @Beck1996], and the depression subscale of the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale [HADS-D, @Zigmond1983] are used for symptom severity, with the Whooley screening [@Whooley1997] and the 2-item version of the PHQ [PHQ-2, @Kroenke2003] used for screening.
Both ask the same questions, answered yes/no or on a Likert scale.
For anxiety disorders, the Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale [GAD-7, @Spitzer2006] is widely used for symptom severity, with the 2-item version (GAD-2) used for screening [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020].
How these recommendations translate into routine practice is less clear.

Systematic use of PROMs at initial assessment and follow-up can improve patient outcomes, particularly in psychological therapy settings [@Clark2018a; @Kendrick2016; @Kendrick2020; @Kendrick2024a; @Gelkopf2022].
The Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) financially incentivised general practitioners to record structured severity assessments for depression at diagnosis from 2006 and at follow-up from 2009, until these indicators were retired in 2013 [@Kendrick2009; @Kendrick2020].
However, large scale research is lacking on the impact of PROMs use on patient trajectories in primary care.
This work first requires reliable codelists that identify PROMs in electronic health records (EHRs) [@Matthewman2024], assessment of recording completeness, including the presence of numeric scores, and distinguishing declined assessments from those never offered.

We set out to describe PROMs recording and use for anxiety disorders and depression in English general practice.
NHS England publishes aggregated [primary care code usage](https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/mi-snomed-code-usage-in-primary-care) data, which includes most general practices in England since `r year(START_DATE)` and is available through the R package *opencodecounts* [@Tamborska2025].
This study aims
(1) to develop open codelists for PROMs based on national guidance,
(2) to describe how often and in what form these measures are recorded over time, and
(3) to show how publicly available aggregate data can inform future patient-level studies.

## Methods

### Design and setting

This was a retrospective descriptive analysis of PROMs-related coding in primary care EHRs.
We analysed national SNOMED CT code usage across all general practices in England that contributed to the public dataset from `r format(START_DATE, "%B %Y")` to `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
The dataset included 6,565 general practices with 63,665,066 registered patients in 2025-26.

### Data sources

We used publicly available [SNOMED CT Code Usage in Primary Care](https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/mi-snomed-code-usage-in-primary-care) data from NHS England, accessed as dataset version `r OCC_GP_DATA_VERSION` through the _opencodecounts_ R package [Version `r OCC_PACKAGE_VERSION`, @Tamborska2025].
SNOMED CT is a standardised clinical terminology that gives each concept a code, a description and a semantic tag for the type of information.
For example, "observable entity" codes record a measurable result (e.g., questionnaire score), and "procedure" codes record an activity (e.g., undertaken assessment).
The usage count reflects the number of times each listed SNOMED CT code was added to a patient's primary care record in England during the annual reporting period, with counts rounded to the nearest 10 and counts of five or below displayed as 5.
Each yearly data point is labelled by its end date (e.g., "July 2024" covers 1 August 2023 to 31 July 2024).

### Codelist development

```{r}
#| label: methods-codelist-development
anx_dep_shared_codes <- intersect(df_anx_proms_cod$code, df_dep_proms_cod$code)
txt_anx_dep_n_shared_codes <- length(anx_dep_shared_codes)
txt_anx_n_codes <- n_distinct(df_anx_proms_cod$code)
txt_anx_n_declined_codes <- n_distinct(df_anx_proms_declined_cod$code)
txt_dep_n_codes <- n_distinct(df_dep_proms_cod$code)
txt_dep_n_declined_codes <- n_distinct(df_dep_proms_declined_cod$code)
txt_anx_shared_overall_pct <- usage_share(df_anx_events, snomed_code %in% anx_dep_shared_codes)
txt_dep_shared_overall_pct <- usage_share(df_dep_events, snomed_code %in% anx_dep_shared_codes)
```

Codelists were created following guidance on codelist development [@Matthewman2024].
We identified search terms and specific SNOMED CT codes from NICE guidelines [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020; @NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2022], the NHS TT manual [@NationalCollaboratingCentreForMentalHealth2024], and the [NHS Primary Care Domain Reference Set](https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/data-collections-and-data-sets/data-collections/quality-and-outcomes-framework-qof/quality-and-outcome-framework-qof-business-rules/primary-care-domain-reference-set-portal) for anxiety and depression screening codes (Supplementary @tbls-anx-dep-nhs-refsets).
We also consulted a general practitioner to identify additional clinically relevant search terms.
For each condition, two codelists were developed: one capturing PROMs activity codes indicating completed assessments and recorded scores, and one capturing declined assessments.
All four codelists developed in this study are published on OpenCodelists and available for reuse (Supplementary @tbls-anx-dep-study-codelists).

**PROMs for anxiety disorders.** The activity codelist included `r txt_anx_n_codes` SNOMED CT codes, including the GAD-7 and GAD-2 [@Spitzer2006], disorder-specific instruments recommended for panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder [@NationalCollaboratingCentreForMentalHealth2024].
The declined assessments codelist included `r txt_anx_n_declined_codes` codes indicating that an assessment was offered but not completed.

**PROMs for depression.** The activity codelist included `r txt_dep_n_codes` SNOMED CT codes, including the PHQ-9 [@Kroenke2001], BDI-II [@Beck1996], and HADS-D [@Zigmond1983], as well as postnatal depression measures, and broader depression screening concepts.
The declined assessments codelist included `r txt_dep_n_declined_codes` codes.

### Data analyses

```{r}
#| label: methods-data-analyses
N_TOP_CODES_TAB <- 10
N_TOP_CODES_FIG <- 3
txt_anx_dep_n_linked_codes <- length(dict_linked_codes)
```

We combined the usage of `r txt_anx_dep_n_linked_codes` pairs of identical codes as specified in the [SNOMED CT History Substitution Table](https://isd.digital.nhs.uk/trud/users/guest/filters/0/categories/8/items/276/releases) or identified by manual review.
We identified the `r N_TOP_CODES_TAB` most frequently recorded codes for the activity and declined codelists for anxiety disorders and depression PROMs.
We plotted the annual activity broken down by semantic tag including "observable entity", "procedure", and all other tags.
Observable entity codes were interpreted as recorded numeric PROMs scores and procedure codes as an indicator for broader assessment activity.
Annual usage counts for the `r N_TOP_CODES_FIG` most frequently recorded activity codes were also plotted.
All analysis code and clinical codelists are openly available at <https://github.com/bennettoxford/proms-primary-care-public-data>.

## Results

### Total PROMs code usage across the study period

```{r}
#| label: results-total-usage
txt_anx_top_overall_pct <- usage_top_share(df_anx_events, N_TOP_CODES_TAB)
txt_dep_top_overall_pct <- usage_top_share(df_dep_events, N_TOP_CODES_TAB)

MAIN_SEMANTIC_TAGS <- c("observable entity", "procedure")

df_anx_events_last <- filter(df_anx_events, year == year(END_DATE))
df_dep_events_last <- filter(df_dep_events, year == year(END_DATE))

txt_anx_score_last_pct <- usage_share(df_anx_events_last, semantic_tag == "observable entity")
txt_dep_score_last_pct <- usage_share(df_dep_events_last, semantic_tag == "observable entity")
txt_dep_proc_last_pct <- usage_share(df_dep_events_last, semantic_tag == "procedure")
txt_anx_other_last_pct <- usage_share(df_anx_events_last, !semantic_tag %in% MAIN_SEMANTIC_TAGS)
txt_dep_other_last_pct <- usage_share(df_dep_events_last, !semantic_tag %in% MAIN_SEMANTIC_TAGS)
```

We identified `r txt_dep_overall` depression-related and `r txt_anx_overall` anxiety disorder-related PROMs recording instances between `r format(START_DATE, "%B %Y")` and `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
For both condition groups, almost all recording instances were captured by the `r N_TOP_CODES_TAB` most frequently used codes, which represented `r txt_anx_top_overall_pct` and `r txt_dep_top_overall_pct` of recording instances for anxiety disorders and depression respectively (@tbl-anx-dep-top).

In `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`, anxiety disorder PROMs recording was predominantly represented by observable entity concepts (`r txt_anx_score_last_pct`), such as "*GAD-7 score*" and "*GAD-2 score*".
Depression PROMs recording was also mainly represented by observable entity concepts (`r txt_dep_score_last_pct`), with fewer procedure concepts (`r txt_dep_proc_last_pct`), such as "*PHQ-9 score*" and "*Depression screening using questions*".
Situation, finding, and assessment scale semantic tag concepts accounted for `r txt_anx_other_last_pct` of anxiety disorder and `r txt_dep_other_last_pct` of depression recorded events.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-anx-dep-top
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: !expr 'paste0("Top ten recorded SNOMED CT PROMs codes for anxiety disorders and depression in England from ", format(START_DATE, "%B %Y"), " to ", format(END_DATE, "%B %Y"), ".")'
#| message: false
#| warning: false
df_tab_anx_dep_top <- df_anx_dep_overall |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = overall_usage,
    n = N_TOP_CODES_TAB,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-type) |>
  mutate(
    semantic_tag = str_to_sentence(semantic_tag),
    description_short = recode(description_short, !!!dict_snomed_description),
    condition = factor(
      condition,
      levels = c("anx", "dep"),
      labels = c(
        "PROMs codes for anxiety disorders",
        "PROMs codes for depression"
      )
    )
  )

tab_anx_dep_top <- df_tab_anx_dep_top |>
  mutate(
    description_short = description_short
  ) |>
  select(-snomed_code) |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    description_short = "Description",
    semantic_tag = "Semantic tag",
    overall_usage = "Usage",
    share_usage = "%"
  ) |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = c(description_short, semantic_tag)) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(overall_usage, share_usage)) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(indent = px(15)),
    locations = cells_body(columns = description_short)
  ) |>
  fmt_number(overall_usage, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = share_usage, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md(
      "*Notes*. GAD = Generalised Anxiety Disorder; HADS = Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale; PHQ = Patient Health Questionnaire; EPDS = Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale; EQ-5D-5L = EuroQol five dimension five level. Percentage usage of PROMs is calculated separately for anxiety disorders and depression, using all recorded events for that condition as the denominator."
    )
  ) |>
  style_manuscript_table()

gtsave(
  tab_anx_dep_top,
  here("output", "tables", "tab-anx-dep-top.png")
)

if (knitr::is_html_output() | knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  tab_anx_dep_top
} else {
  knitr::include_graphics(here(
    "output",
    "tables",
    "tab-anx-dep-top.png"
  ))
}
```

### Annual trends in overall PROMs recording

```{r}
#| label: results-annual-trends-overall
txt_dep_2012 <- usage_total(df_dep_events, year == 2012)
txt_dep_2014 <- usage_total(df_dep_events, year == 2014)
txt_dep_proc_2012 <- usage_total(
  df_dep_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "procedure",
  year == 2012
)
txt_dep_proc_last <- usage_total(
  df_dep_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "procedure",
  year == year(END_DATE)
)
txt_dep_score_2012 <- usage_total(
  df_dep_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "observable entity",
  year == 2012
)
txt_dep_score_2016 <- usage_total(
  df_dep_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "observable entity",
  year == 2016
)
txt_dep_score_last <- usage_total(
  df_dep_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "observable entity",
  year == year(END_DATE)
)
txt_anx_score_2012 <- usage_total(
  df_anx_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "observable entity",
  year == 2012
)
txt_anx_score_last <- usage_total(
  df_anx_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "observable entity",
  year == year(END_DATE)
)

txt_anx_proc_max <- usage_max(
  df_anx_events,
  type == "activity",
  semantic_tag == "procedure",
  .by = year
)
txt_anx_declined_max <- usage_max(df_anx_events, type == "declined", .by = year)
txt_dep_declined_max <- usage_max(df_dep_events, type == "declined", .by = year)

txt_anx_dep_declined_one_in_last_rounded <- df_anx_dep_events |>
  filter(year == year(END_DATE)) |>
  summarise(one_in = sum(usage) / sum(usage[type == "declined"])) |>
  pull(one_in) |>
  round()
```

Annual trends showed higher depression-related PROMs coding than anxiety disorder-related coding throughout the study period.
However, depression-related PROMs coding declined from `r txt_dep_2012` recorded events in July 2012 to `r txt_dep_2014` by July 2014, increasing slowly to `r txt_dep_last` in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
In contrast, anxiety disorder PROMs recording remained lower but increased over time, reaching `r txt_anx_last` recorded events by `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (@fig-anx-dep-trends, Panel A).

PROMs for depression were initially most often recorded as procedures, but this declined substantially from `r txt_dep_proc_2012` in July 2012 to `r txt_dep_proc_last` in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (@fig-anx-dep-trends, Panel C).
Depression-related PROMs with scores (observable entity) declined from `r txt_dep_score_2012` in July 2012 to `r txt_dep_score_2016` in July 2016, before increasing again to `r txt_dep_score_last` by `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (@fig-anx-dep-trends, Panel B).
Anxiety disorder PROMs were rarely recorded as procedures, with no more than `r txt_anx_proc_max` recorded events in any year, while codes with scores increased from `r txt_anx_score_2012` in July 2012 to `r txt_anx_score_last` in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (@fig-anx-dep-trends, Panel B-C).
Together, these trends show a shift from procedure codes towards observable entity codes recording numeric PROMs scores, most evident for depression.
Declined PROMs recording increased over the study period but remained low, reaching at most `r txt_dep_declined_max` recorded events in any year for depression and `r txt_anx_declined_max` for anxiety disorders (Supplementary @figs-anx-dep-declined).
This represented 1 in `r txt_anx_dep_declined_one_in_last_rounded` recorded PROMs codes by `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-anx-dep-trends
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Yearly recorded events for PROMs codes for anxiety disorders and depression in English general practice from ", format(START_DATE, "%B %Y"), " to ", format(END_DATE, "%B %Y"), ". (A) Total PROMs coding, including all activity and declined codes; (B) score codes, which are observable entity concepts representing recorded PROM scores; and (C) procedure codes, representing PROM administration. No procedure code events were recorded for anxiety disorders before 2013. Panels B and C share the same y-axis range, which differs from Panel A.")'
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 8
#| warning: false
fig_anx_dep_total <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  plot_usage_trend(
    x = end_date,
    y = usage,
    group = condition_label,

fig_anx_dep_obs_ent <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  filter(type == "activity", semantic_tag == "observable entity") |>
  plot_usage_trend(
    x = end_date,

fig_anx_dep_proc <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  filter(type == "activity", semantic_tag == "procedure") |>
  plot_usage_trend(
    x = end_date,
    y = usage,
    group = condition_label,
    panel_label = "PROMs coded as procedures",
    x_breaks = x_breaks
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = .6)

y_max_obs_ent_proc <- max(
  fig_anx_dep_obs_ent$data$.usage,

)

fig_anx_dep_trends <- (fig_anx_dep_total /

  plot_layout(guides = "collect", axis_titles = "collect") +

fig_anx_dep_trends
```

Among the PROMs codes for anxiety disorders, "*GAD-7 score*" was the most frequently recorded code throughout the study period and increased overall from July 2012 to `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")` (@fig-anx-dep-top-trends, Panel A).
"*GAD-2 score*" recording appeared from July 2019 and increased thereafter.
Both codes showed their most rapid increases from 2023.
The remaining code ("*HADS anxiety score*") was recorded at lower volumes, with no more than `r txt_anx_hads_max` recorded events per year.

For the two most frequently used depression-related PROMs codes, recording declined between July 2012 and July 2014.
However "*Depression screening using questions*" continued to decrease to `r txt_dep_screen_last` by `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`, whereas "*PHQ-9 score*" increased again to `r txt_dep_phq9_last`, above its level of `r txt_dep_phq9_2012` in July 2012, the year before the QOF financial incentives for using PROMs were discontinued (@fig-anx-dep-top-trends, Panel B).
In July `r txt_dep_phq9_overtakes_year`, "*PHQ-9 score*" was recorded more often than "*Depression screening using questions*" for the first time.
The remaining top depression PROMs code ("*PHQ-2 score*") was first recorded in July `r txt_dep_phq2_first_year` and increased to `r txt_dep_phq2_last` by `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
In July `r txt_dep_phq2_overtakes_year`, it was recorded more often than "*Depression screening using questions*" for the first time.

Short measures (PHQ-2, GAD-2, 4-item PHQ [PHQ-4] and Whooley screening) made up `r txt_anx_short_last_pct` of anxiety disorder and `r txt_dep_short_last_pct` of depression activity coding in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`, up from `r txt_anx_short_2012_pct` and `r txt_dep_short_2012_pct` in July 2012.

## Discussion

### Summary

Using publicly available aggregate data, we described coding patterns for PROMs for anxiety disorders and depression in primary care records from `r year(START_DATE)` to `r year(END_DATE)`.
Over the past 5 years, GAD-7 and PHQ-9 were the most frequently recorded PROMs annually for anxiety disorders and depression respectively.
While "*Depression screening using questions*" had the highest cumulative recording across the study period, "*PHQ-9 score*" was the most frequently recorded code annually from July `r txt_dep_phq9_overtakes_year` onwards.
Depression-related PROMs coding was consistently higher than anxiety disorder-related coding.
Over the study period, recording shifted from broader procedure codes towards named PROMs score codes, most evident for depression.

### Comparison with existing literature

Consistent with previous research [@Kendrick2009], most activity of assessing symptom severity in primary care was captured by a small number of PROMs.
Although the NICE-recommended PHQ-9 and GAD-2 appeared among the most frequently used codes [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2022; @NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020], the codes with the highest overall usage were the GAD-7 for anxiety disorders and "Depression screening using questions" for depression, in line with reported variation in PROMs use across general practice [@Turner2020].
Of the three depression measures recommended for general practice use [@BritishMedicalAssociation2006], the PHQ-9 and HADS-D appeared among the most frequently recorded codes.
This is consistent with assessment patterns observed under QOF, where the PHQ-9 accounted for most assessments [@Kendrick2009].
The high use of PHQ-9 and GAD-7 may also reflect their role as standard outcome measures in NHS TT [@NationalCollaboratingCentreForMentalHealth2024].
Although disorder-specific measures are recommended for conditions such as posttraumatic stress disorder [@NationalCollaboratingCentreForMentalHealth2024], these instruments were rarely recorded in general practice.

Depression PROMs coding was consistently highest across the study period, potentially reflecting the earlier financial incentives [@Kendrick2009; @Kendrick2020].
The early decline in depression coding we observed coincided with the removal of the incentive in 2013 [@Kendrick2009; @Kendrick2020].
NICE guidance continued to recommend the use of routine outcome monitoring [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2022], which may partly explain the persistence of PHQ-9 recording.
PHQ-9 score recording recovered to levels above those observed under QOF incentivisation.
Possible explanations include psychological services placing greater value on symptom scores for referred patients, or changes in how symptom questionnaires are used in primary care.
For example, recorded remote consultations in English general practice more than tripled during the COVID-19 pandemic [@Aminu2025].
Patient communication platforms enable patients to complete PROMs remotely, with scores written into the patient's EHR, including PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores [@Davies2026].

The increased coding of PROMs for anxiety disorders from 2011, particularly GAD-2 and GAD-7, is consistent with NICE recommendations to consider the GAD-2 and to monitor outcomes with short questionnaires [@NationalInstituteForHealthAndCareExcellence2020].
The increase in anxiety disorder PROMs coding parallels broader increases in recorded anxiety diagnoses and symptoms in UK primary care from around 2011 [@Archer2022; @Slee2021].
In addition, the estimated prevalence in England was higher for generalised anxiety disorder compared to depressive episodes in 2023/24 [@Morris2025].
Nevertheless, anxiety disorder PROMs coding remained lower than depression PROMs coding.
The discrepancy may reflect differences in the clinical pathways and incentives surrounding the assessment and monitoring of anxiety disorders and depression in primary care.

A further pattern was a shift away from broader procedure codes towards named PROMs score codes, which better indicate what was assessed and may improve interpretability.
NICE recommends the Whooley screening in yes/no form, but PHQ-2 scores were recorded about `r txt_dep_phq2_whooley_ratio_last_rounded` times as often as Whooley codes in `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
<!-- TODO Milan: decide how to word this. Whooley screening may have been done and recorded under a generic code such as "Depression screening using questions", so we do not know how often it was used. That code cannot record a yes/no answer. -->
Short measures are designed as a first step and not to monitor severity [@Kroenke2003], so their increase may not reflect better outcome monitoring.
In 2016, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence that routine PROMs monitoring improves outcomes in common mental health disorders, with only two of 17 studies conducted in primary care [@Kendrick2016].
Since then, a cluster randomised trial in English and Welsh general practices found no significant effect of PHQ-9 monitoring on depression symptom outcomes, although patients' quality of life improved and in a post-hoc per-protocol analysis, recording of follow-up PHQ-9 scores led to more changes of treatment and referrals [@Kendrick2024a].
Given the substantial growth in PROMs recording in general practice since 2016, national studies using patient-level data could re-evaluate the impact of PROMs on patient outcomes in routine care.

### Strengths and limitations

The main strength of this study is its national scale.
The codelists developed for this study are openly available on OpenCodelists and can be reused in future patient-level work using EHRs.
This study also demonstrates how the *opencodecounts* R package [@Tamborska2025] can be used to study PROMs recording activity in general practice using only publicly available aggregate data, without applying for patient-level data extracts from NHS England.

The main limitation is that this study used aggregate counts of recorded code usage, rather than patient-level data.
This means we cannot distinguish how often PROMs are used per patient and how this may change over time. However, it is likely that individual PROMs codes on the whole are representative of unique PROMs completion events, for example the same patient completing the PHQ-9 at different appointments.
It is also difficult to disentangle broader changes in clinical coding trends from clinical practice trends in recording, especially when there are no financial incentives to record activities.
Some PROMs-related information may be recorded in free text clinical notes rather than structured codes, so the analysis may undercapture the number of PROMs used.
Before 2019, data was submitted in Read v2 or CTV3 format and was mapped to SNOMED CT, which may affect the comparability of counts across the full study period.
We also cannot determine how PROMs codes were added to primary care records.
For example, whether the codes were imported from patient applications that were completed online, external services such as NHS TT, or recorded during primary care consultations.
We also cannot tell whether short measures were used alone or recorded alongside a full measure.
The use of generic codes, such as "*Depression screening using questions*", creates uncertainty about which specific PROM was administered.

### Implications for research and practice

The increase in "*PHQ-9 score*" and "*GAD-7 score*" recording means that general practice now increasingly records the same measures used as outcomes in NHS TT.
Patient-level linkage of primary care and NHS TT records would allow symptom severity to be analysed across both settings.
The codelists developed in this study identify PROMs recording in primary care records and can be used for these analyses.

NHS England also publishes aggregated PROMs outcomes from NHS TT, where the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and Work and Social Adjustment Scale [WSAS, @Mundt2002] are collected as standard measures at every treatment session [@NationalCollaboratingCentreForMentalHealth2024].
These measures are recorded for 98% of patients who received treatment with a score recorded at the start and end of treatment.
The published outcomes are broken down by therapy type and main mental health problem [@Clark2018a].
In psychological therapy services there is good evidence that routine outcome monitoring improves patient outcomes [@Kendrick2020; @Delgadillo2021].
The *nhstt* R package [@Wiedemann2026] provides access to this data in an analysis-ready format and could be used to describe how symptom severity at the start and end of treatment has changed over time and varies across services.

### Conclusion

Recording of anxiety disorders and depression severity in English general practice is captured by a small number of PROMs and has shifted towards named score codes.
Recording declined after depression incentives were withdrawn in 2013, then increased again for both conditions in recent years.
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores are now the most used measures, matching the outcome measures used in NHS TT.
Publicly available aggregate data can be used to describe this activity and inform future patient-level research on PROMs in routine care.

::: {#tbls-anx-dep-study-codelists}

```{r}
#| label: make-tab-anx-dep-study-codelists
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

df_tab_anx_dep_study_codelists <- tribble(
  ~condition, ~codelist_name, ~opencodelists_id,
  "Anxiety Disorders", "PROMs activity", "[user/Lola_O/proms-anx/1ed7683b/](https://www.opencodelists.org/codelist/user/Lola_O/proms-anx/1ed7683b/)",
  "Anxiety Disorders", "PROMs declined", "[user/Lola_O/proms-anx-declined/631bb866/](https://www.opencodelists.org/codelist/user/Lola_O/proms-anx-declined/631bb866/)",
  "Depression", "PROMs activity", "[user/Lola_O/proms-dep/05c7f506/](https://www.opencodelists.org/codelist/user/Lola_O/proms-dep/05c7f506/)",
  "Depression", "PROMs declined", "[user/Lola_O/proms-dep-declined/4a0c4531/](https://www.opencodelists.org/codelist/user/Lola_O/proms-dep-declined/4a0c4531/)"
)

tab_anx_dep_study_codelists <- df_tab_anx_dep_study_codelists |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    codelist_name = "Codelist name",
    opencodelists_id = "OpenCodelists ID"
  ) |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = everything()) |>
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(indent = px(15)),
    locations = cells_body(columns = codelist_name)
  ) |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = opencodelists_id) |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md(paste0(
      "*Notes.* Codelist IDs link directly to the corresponding codelist on OpenCodelists. The activity codelists share ",
      txt_anx_dep_n_shared_codes,
      " codes, such as the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, but these account for only ",
      txt_anx_shared_overall_pct,
      " of anxiety disorder and ",
      txt_dep_shared_overall_pct,
      " of depression recorded events."
    ))
  ) |>
  style_manuscript_table()

gtsave(
  tab_anx_dep_study_codelists,
  here("output", "tables", "tab-anx-dep-study-codelists.png")
)

# gt's LaTeX table cannot sit inside the custom tbls float, so PDF uses the PNG
if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  tab_anx_dep_study_codelists
} else {
  knitr::include_graphics(here(
    "output",
    "tables",
    "tab-anx-dep-study-codelists.png"
  ))
}
```

PROMs activity and declined codelists for anxiety disorders and depression developed in this study
:::

::: {#figs-anx-dep-declined}

```{r}
#| label: make-fig-anx-dep-declined
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 8
#| warning: false

fig_anx_dep_declined <- df_anx_dep_usage |>
  filter(type == "declined") |>
  plot_usage_trend(
    x = end_date,
    y = usage,
    group = condition_label,
    panel_label = "PROMs coded as declined",
    x_breaks = x_breaks
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = .6) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, byrow = TRUE),
    shape = guide_legend(nrow = 1, byrow = TRUE)
  )

ggsave(
  filename = here(
    "output",
    "figures",
    "fig-anx-dep-declined.png"
  ),
  fig_anx_dep_declined,
  height = 4,
  width = 8
)

fig_anx_dep_declined
```

Yearly recorded events for declined PROMs codes for anxiety disorders and depression in English general practice from `r format(START_DATE, "%B %Y")` to `r format(END_DATE, "%B %Y")`.
